records.name_note: Admissible sources agree on the common name but split on the accepted binomial. On common name: NC State's Plant Toolbox renders a "Common Name(s):" list whose first item is "Celandine Poppy" (Wood poppy, Woods-poppy, Yellow Wood Poppy follow); Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder shows a single visible "Common Name:" line reading "celandine poppy", with a hover/click info popup behind it listing three names -- celandine poppy, flaming poppy, wood poppy -- celandine poppy first; RHS's dedicated species page carries the H1 as the botanical name alone, with the plant-profile subtitle and its "Other common names" field both leading with "celandine poppy" (followed by "wood poppy"). On the binomial: RHS's dedicated page for this taxon (canonical URL /plants/538059/chelidonium-diphyllum/details) gives "Name Status" as "Correct" for Chelidonium diphyllum, placing it in genus Chelidonium, and lists "Stylophorum diphyllum" only as a Synonym -- i.e. RHS has sunk Stylophorum into Chelidonium for this species. NC State's Plant Toolbox and Missouri Botanical Garden's Plant Finder both continue to treat "Stylophorum diphyllum" itself as the accepted binomial (genus Stylophorum) and do not mention Chelidonium diphyllum at all. scientific_name_accepted above follows RHS's Name-Status-Correct binomial per the field-support rule, but a user should be told the other two admissible sources have not adopted this merger. Under RHS's placement the accepted binomial Chelidonium diphyllum sits in the same genus as Chelidonium majus (Greater Celandine) -- the weedy species NC State flags as often confused with this plant and rates Poison Severity High -- but they are different plants: Chelidonium diphyllum is NOT Greater Celandine.
unknowns: is_houseplant: left null -- every admissible source (NC State, MoBoT, RHS) frames this species purely as an outdoor woodland/shade-garden perennial (naturalized areas, streambanks, woodland gardens); none explicitly states whether it is or is not suitable as a houseplant, so no field-level claim could be built without inferring beyond the sources.

toxic_to_pets and toxicity_detail: left null. None of the three admissible pages that carry a dedicated profile for this exact species (NC State Plant Toolbox, MoBoT Plant Finder, RHS) include any Poison/toxicity block, cat- or dog-scoped or otherwise, for Stylophorum diphyllum -- NC State's page for this species has no 'Poison' section at all (that structured toxicity apparatus exists on NC State's page for the confused-with species Chelidonium majus, not for this one). The only toxicity information found for S. diphyllum concerns skin/dye staining from its yellow-orange sap (NC State: 'Contact with the sap can stain your skin'; MoBoT: sap 'formerly used as a dye by Native Americans'), which is not a poisoning claim and not animal-scoped, so it cannot support toxic_to_pets either way.

records.name_note: Sources split on which common name is primary for Packera aurea. NC State's browser title reads "Packera aurea (Butterweed, Golden Groundsel, Golden Ragwort)"; its on-page "Common Name(s):" list renders three separate entries -- "Butterweed", "Golden Groundsel", "Golden Ragwort" -- in that order, so Golden Ragwort is third. RHS's plant-profile subtitle for this species reads "false valerian"; "golden ragwort" appears only inside RHS's secondary "Other common names" field ("false valerian, golden groundsel, golden ragwort, life root"), not the subtitle. MoBot's dedicated single "Common Name" field, by contrast, reads "golden ragwort" directly ("Common Name: golden ragwort"), and that field was used to set common_name here. All three of the naming sources cited here (NC State, RHS, MoBot) record the former name Senecio aureus: NC State under its "Previously known as:" heading, RHS under Synonyms, and MoBot in prose ("Synonymous with Senecio aureus.").
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's toxicity block for Packera aurea is explicitly headed "Poisonous to Humans:" (human-scoped, not pet-scoped), and states the plant "has low severity poison characteristics." Within that block: Poison Severity is "Low"; Poison Part is "Leaves" (the full and only part listed); Poison Symptoms are "Liver toxicity; skin irritation following contact."; Poison Toxic Principle is "Pyrrolizidine alkaloids"; and Causes Contact Dermatitis is "Yes." The same page's Plant Type tags separately co-list "Poisonous" alongside "Ground Cover," "Herbaceous Perennial," "Native Plant," and "Wildflower." No admissible source (NC State, Clemson HGIC, MoBot, UF/IFAS, RHS, PSU, UMD, or UGA fieldreport) scopes this toxicity to cats or dogs specifically, nor lists any Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag for this species, so toxic_to_pets is left unconfirmed (see unknowns).
unknowns: toxic_to_pets left null: no admissible source scopes Packera aurea's pyrrolizidine-alkaloid toxicity to cats or dogs specifically. NC State's poison block is explicitly headed 'Poisonous to Humans:' and no admissible page for this species carries a Problem-for-Cats or Problem-for-Dogs tag, so a cats/dogs-specific finding could not be confirmed.
is_houseplant left null: every admissible source describes Packera aurea only as an outdoor native woodland/groundcover perennial; none states whether it is suitable or used as an indoor houseplant.

NC State's Light tags carry generic legend hour ranges (e.g. '6 or more hours', '2-6 hours') but these are the site-wide category legend, not species-specific prose, so per instructions they were not used for direct_sun_hours_max.

outdoor_sun_exposure excludes full_shade: UMD's Sun field ('Sun: part sun to full shade') names full shade, but NC State's Light field (only 'Full sun' and 'Partial Shade' tags) and MoBot's Sun field ('Full sun to part shade') both cap the range at part shade, so full_shade was left out per the tie-break rule and is disclosed here.

soil_ph_min left null: NC State's Soil pH tag for Packera aurea, 'Acid (<6.0)', is an open-ended band with no floor. PSU's 'Soil: Acidic (pH < 6.8)' supplied only a ceiling (used for soil_ph_max). RHS's page for this species carries no populated soil pH field to cross-check the ceiling against.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, and water_estimate_basis are left null: Packera aurea is an in-ground perennial, and no admissible source frames its watering in dry-down, check-depth, or day-interval terms.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, and fertilize_strength are left null: no admissible source (NC State, MoBot, RHS, UMD, PSU, UF/IFAS, Clemson HGIC, or UGA fieldreport) discusses fertilizing Packera aurea.

MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium to wet' field is noted as consistent with, not contradicting, the keep_moist water_regime reading, since it spans into 'wet' rather than being a bare mid-scale 'Medium' reading (which per instructions would not by itself support keep_moist).

Clemson HGIC and UGA fieldreport (caes.uga.edu) admissible-domain searches did not surface a dedicated Packera aurea page with fetchable, quotable content distinct from what NC State/MoBot/UMD/PSU/RHS already provided, so they are not cited here despite being in the admissible domain list.

records.name_note: All four admissible dedicated-page sources agree Cardinal Flower/cardinal flower is the primary common name, but they structure their common-name fields differently. NC State lists three names under a single Common Name(s) field, Cardinal Flower first, with no separate primary/secondary split. RHS's H1 is the botanical name alone ("Lobelia cardinalis"); "cardinal flower" appears in the page title and the plant-profile subtitle, while a separate "Other common names" field lists eight further alternates (including "Indian pink") that RHS does not treat as the page's lead name. MoBot's Plant Finder leads with a Common Name field reading "cardinal flower", and the eight-name list behind its Common Names control also puts "cardinal flower" first. Clemson HGIC's article is titled and led by "Cardinal Flower" as well. So "Indian Pink," which NC State lists second and RHS relegates to its secondary Other-common-names field, is never the lead name of any admissible dedicated page and is not used as common_name here.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's "Poisonous to Humans" block (a human-scoped heading, distinct from its separate Problem-for-Cats/Problem-for-Dogs tags) rates Poison Severity: Medium, and the page header reads "This plant has medium severity poison characteristics." Poison Symptoms: "TOXIC ONLY IF LARGE QUANTITIES EATEN. Nausea, depression, vomiting, diarrhea, salivation, exhaustion and weakness, dilation of pupils, convulsions, and coma, abdominal pain, heart rhythm disturbances." Poison Toxic Principle: "Alkaloids lobelamine, lobeline, and others, plus a volatile oil." Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part (full list, not truncated): Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. Separately, under NC State's "Problems" tags the plant is flagged Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, and Problem for Horses -- the cat/dog designation is a distinct tag from the human-scoped severity rating above -- and NC State also carries "Poisonous" among its Whole Plant Traits > Plant Type values. Missouri Botanical Garden frames the hazard more strongly than NC State's hedged Medium rating: "Foliage contains alkaloids which are very toxic to humans if ingested." The two sources disagree on severity, not on the fact of toxicity. RHS's "Potentially harmful" field adds a handling warning and names skin irritation as well as ingestion risk: "Harmful if eaten; skin irritant. Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling. Pets: Harmful if eaten; skin irritant. For further information and contact numbers regarding pets, see the HTA guide to potentially harmful plants". RHS's "Pets" mention does not itself name cats or dogs specifically, so on its own it would not establish cat/dog-scoped risk -- that scoping comes from NC State's explicit Problem-for-Cats and Problem-for-Dogs tags.
